# DevLink365

**Share your localhost with anyone.**

You have something running on `localhost`. DevLink365 gives you a link.

```bash
npx devlink365
```

```
  ✓ DevLink365 is running

  Local:  http://localhost:3000
  Public: https://a8f3k2qd.devlink365.dev

  Expires: in 4 hours
  Relay:   relay.devlink365.dev

  Anyone with the link can reach your local app. Press Ctrl+C to stop sharing.
```

Send that URL to a designer, a client, a teammate, or your own phone. They see
the app running on your machine. No deployment, no account, no config.

- **Zero configuration** — it finds your dev server and picks the port for you
- **Zero runtime dependencies** — Node 18.17+ and nothing else
- **Temporary by design** — every link expires, 24 hours at the very most
- **Framework agnostic** — Next.js, Vite, Rails, Django, a plain `python -m http.server`
- **Works behind NAT and VPNs** — the connection is outbound only
- **WebSockets included** — hot module reload keeps working through the tunnel

---

## Install

You don't. Run it:

```bash
npx devlink365
```

Install it globally if you use it constantly:

```bash
npm install -g devlink365
```

---

## Usage

Start your app first — DevLink365 shares a server, it doesn't start one.

```bash
npm run dev          # terminal 1
npx devlink365       # terminal 2
```

### Options

| Flag | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-p, --port <number>` | Port your app is on | detected |
| `--host <host>` | Local host to forward to | `127.0.0.1` |
| `-e, --expires <time>` | Link lifetime: `30m`, `4h`, `24h` | `4h` (max `24h`) |
| `-n, --name <label>` | Prefix for the subdomain | random |
| `--relay <url>` | Relay to use | `wss://relay.devlink365.dev` |
| `--json` | Print one JSON line and stay quiet | off |
| `-q, --quiet` | Don't log individual requests | off |
| `--no-rewrite-host` | Pass the public `Host` through to your app | off |
| `--insecure` | Skip TLS verification (self-hosted relays only) | off |
| `-y, --yes` | Don't ask for confirmation | off |

### Examples

```bash
npx devlink365                                  # find the server, share it for 4 hours
npx devlink365 --port 5173                      # be explicit about the port
npx devlink365 --expires 30m                    # a short-lived link
npx devlink365 --name checkout-demo --expires 24h
npx devlink365 --json                           # for scripts and CI
```

`--name` is a prefix, not a promise: DevLink365 always appends random characters,
so `--name checkout-demo` gives you something like `checkout-demo-k7m2xq`. A
guessable name must never produce a guessable URL.

---

## How it works

```
your machine                          the internet
─────────────                         ────────────

  localhost:3000
        ▲
        │  http
        │
   devlink365  ──── outbound wss ────▶  relay.devlink365.dev
   (this CLI)                                  │
                                               │  https
                                               ▼
                                   a8f3k2qd.devlink365.dev
                                               │
                                               ▼
                                          your visitor
```

The CLI opens **one outbound WebSocket** to the relay. Every visitor request is
multiplexed down that connection, replayed against your local server, and
streamed back. Nothing ever dials in to your machine, which is why this works
from behind NAT, a VPN, or a corporate firewall with no port forwarding.

When the CLI exits, the connection closes and the URL stops working —
immediately, not eventually.

---

## Using it as a library

```ts
import { createTunnel } from "devlink365";

const tunnel = await createTunnel({ port: 3000, ttlMs: 60 * 60 * 1000 });
console.log(tunnel.details?.url);

tunnel.on("request", ({ method, url, status }) => {
  console.log(method, url, status);
});

// later
tunnel.stop();
```

Useful in CI: open a tunnel, hand the URL to a webhook provider or a visual
regression service, tear it down when the job ends.

---

## Security

DevLink365 exposes a development server to the public internet. That is the
point, and it is also the risk. What the tool does about it:

- **Unguessable URLs.** Ids are drawn from `crypto.randomBytes` over a 28-symbol
  alphabet — roughly 38 bits, and a label never removes the random part.
- **Everything expires.** The default is 4 hours and the ceiling is 24, enforced
  by the relay rather than the client.
- **Ctrl+C is final.** Closing the CLI closes the tunnel and kills the URL.
- **HTTPS only** on the public side.
- **Reserved names.** `www`, `api`, `admin`, `login` and friends can never
  become a tunnel subdomain.
- **One level of subdomain.** `a.b.devlink365.dev` is never routed, so nothing
  slips past a wildcard certificate.
- **Non-HTTP ports are not auto-selected.** If port 5432 is open, detection will
  not quietly publish your database.
- **Body and rate limits.** 25 MB per request, per-visitor request ceilings, and
  caps on concurrent tunnels per source address.

What it does **not** do yet: password protection, visitor authentication, and
request inspection. Those are on the roadmap. Until then, treat a DevLink365 URL
as public — anyone who has it can reach your app, so don't point one at
something holding real credentials or production data.

## Running your own relay

The relay ships in the same package.

```bash
npx devlink365-server --domain tunnels.example.com --trust-proxy
```

```bash
npx devlink365 --relay wss://tunnels.example.com
```

You need two DNS records pointing at the relay — `tunnels.example.com` and
`*.tunnels.example.com` — and a wildcard certificate. Terminating TLS at
Cloudflare, Caddy, or a load balancer is the easy path; just make sure it
forwards WebSocket upgrades and start the relay with `--trust-proxy` so rate
limits see the real visitor address.

Run `npx devlink365-server --help` for every option.

---

## What DevLink365 is not (yet)

This is the first version, and it does one thing: turns localhost into a link.
Planned, but **not built**:

- password protection and visitor authentication
- QR codes and mobile previews
- request and session inspection, webhook testing
- inviting teammates and clients, shared state, annotations
- AI-assisted debugging of what went through the tunnel

---

## Requirements

Node.js 18.17 or newer.
